# Project Phoenix — Implementation plan

This file sets out how to build the world of `docs/PROJECT_PHOENIX.md`, step by step, on the architecture of
`docs/ARCHITECTURE.md`: the spec says **what**, the architecture says **how**, and this file says exactly what to
build, in what order, how to know it is right and what is not allowed on the way, so that a builder who has never
seen the project can take the next step and finish it without inventing anything. Every base the finished world
needs — every store, kernel and index, for every stage — is built first, in Stage 1's core, designed for its last
user and measured at the design point; every later step only activates those bases with rules, decisions and
declared data. Where this file and the architecture disagree, the architecture is fixed first, in its own change,
and this file follows; where either disagrees with the spec, the spec wins.

---

## 0. How to use this file

### 0.1 The rules of the work

1. **Bases first.** Every store, kernel and index any stage needs is a core step of Stage 1 (§1), built and measured
   at the design point before behaviour is put on it. A behaviour step only activates bases: it adds rules,
   decisions, declared data and routing (§2.22), never a store, index, map, kernel or per-party pass of its own.
2. **One step at a time, in order.**
   - Take the first step whose status is `planned` and set it to `building`.
   - Finish it — every item of its **Done when** — before touching the next.
   - Never have two steps in `building`.
3. **Read before writing.**
   - Before the first line of a step's code, read the spec's laws (Part I), Part II, the clauses the step lists, the
     sections of every system in their **Depends on** line, and the architecture sections the step lists.
   - Read every earlier step it depends on, as built, and the bases it activates.
   - Whatever these do not settle is settled by the laws. If the laws do not settle it and it is a decision the spec
     reserves to the owner (§0.6), ask, and stop that step until it is answered. Anything else the builder derives
     from the spec and states in the commit.
   - Where a clause and a law disagree, the clause is wrong: it is fixed in its own change, saying why.
4. **Build exactly what the step says.**
   - Its files, types, layouts, algorithms and declarations are the design.
   - A better idea becomes a change to this file in its own commit, before any code follows it.
   - Code never runs ahead of this file, and the spec and the architecture are updated in the same change as the
     thing they describe.
5. **Never weaken an earlier step.**
   - A later step extends a base only through the extension points the base's step declared (its **Extension
     points**).
   - A change to a base's layout or public surface is itself a step, inserted at its dependency position (§0.4).
   - A need no extension point covers is a new base step before the step that needs it, never absorbed into it.
6. **When a step is done.**
   - Every step: the fast checks (`cargo fmt --check`, `cargo clippy`, the tests, `phx-check all`).
   - Every step that changes code or data: also the bench's read of the budget at the committed resolution (§2.10),
     with no ratchet broken unless the step says why; a step that changes only the opening reads the opening's span
     against its ratchet. A `docs` step, which changes no code or data, is exempt.
   - A base, kernel or index: also its finished-volume measure, `tools/bench.sh -F <base>`, at the design point,
     within its ratchets (§2.22).
   - A gate: also the gate run and criteria of §2.24.
   - Live checks run at a step only when its **Done when** names them (`tools/bench.sh -c`).
7. **Two reviews.** Every step ends with two reviews of its diff, with the prompts of §0.7:
   - one reads the diff against the spec's clauses and laws and this step's text;
   - the other reads it against the architecture, the budget, the bases' discipline and this step's **Not allowed**.

   At a **major step** — a stage's gate, or a step the owner names — the two are independent: fresh agents who did
   not write it. At any other step the builder makes both passes itself, one prompt at a time. Every finding is
   fixed in the step (§0.5). Only then is the step done.
8. **Commits.** One change, one commit, saying what and why, with the step's identifier as its first word
   (`S1.159: …`). The step's last commit:
   - moves whatever needs keeping about how it was built into `docs/ARCHITECTURE.md`;
   - removes the step's whole section from this file, leaving its rows in §13;
   - regenerates the coverage table (`phx-check coverage --write`);
   - writes the ratchets the step moves in `perf/budget.toml` or `perf/ratchets.toml`, each with its reason.

### 0.2 The shape of a step

Every step has these sections, in this order; `phx-check docs` refuses a step missing one or holding them out of
order (PC-09). A `retired` step needs only its **Status**.

| Section | What it says |
| --- | --- |
| **Status** | `planned`, `building`, `awaiting owner` (its remaining **Done when** items the owner's alone), `held` (begun and set aside while an earlier step, reopened, is building) or `retired`; a word, and at most one clause of reason |
| **Kind** | one word from the list below |
| **Clauses** | `SYS.n TYPE; SYS.m TYPE *(part: what it carries)*`, items separated by `; `, the TYPE on every item, laws as `Law n *(part)*`, and nothing else on the line (`none` alone when it completes nothing; a clause it only carries or serves is one sentence in **Design**). Its completed clauses equal its rows in §13 |
| **Architecture** | the architecture sections it writes or follows; a base step writes its own section |
| **Depends on** | earlier steps only, each with its reason (`S1.160 (the accounts' columns)`), and the bases it reads or writes |
| **Goal** | two or three sentences, present tense: what exists after |
| **Files** | a table `\| path \| purpose \|` of every file created or changed, crate paths in full (`crates/<layer>/<crate>/src/…`), a base's `phx-fin` module, and the data series (manifest keys) it maps |
| **Design** | types with field sizes; layouts; algorithms precise enough to code from; declarations. For a mechanism: the rule's inputs (views of which bases), its outputs (writes through which base's API, or flows under which declared reason), when it runs (due, woken, occasion) and its streams. The placeholders it introduces, each naming the step that retires it, and those it retires. No measured narrative, dates, history or commit hashes |
| **Edge cases** | each case of §2.23 that applies, how it is met, and the unit test (by name) or `LC-` id that shows it; an item that rests on a base's guarantee cites that base's test by name |
| **Extension points** | a base, kernel or index: every later step and clause that reads or writes it, and the declared data or API each uses. Any other step: `none`, or the points it adds |
| **Unit tests** | logic-level tests by name, each asserting arithmetic or a refusal (§2.9) |
| **Live checks** | `LC-` identifiers, what each reads on the running world and the event that makes it applicable; or `none` |
| **Budget** | a base, kernel or index: its volumes at the design point on an ordinary business (B), non-business (NB) and heavy (H) day; its access pattern (due-driven, event, rolling slice); its unit target in phone ns and VM ns; its miss budget; bytes a row and MB at the design point; its traversal (columns, party ranges on the pool, sharding); the ratchets it adds under `perf/budget.toml [fin.<base>]`. A mechanism: `B / NB / H counts × unit ns → core-ms`, the base operations it spends, and "its share of <stage line>: x / y / z core-ms (B / NB / H)"; its resident bytes as a line of ARCHITECTURE §13's memory ledger; the counters it adds |
| **Guards** | the `phx-check` rules, clippy lists and assembly refusals it adds |
| **Not allowed** | for every step that is not a base, kernel or index: "a store, index, map or per-party pass outside the core bases"; "a pass over every party every day"; "an allocation per day"; then the step's own temptations, named so a reviewer can look for them |
| **Done when** | a checklist, each item verifiable: the code and its tests; the fast checks; the bench's budget read (not for a `docs` step); for a base, kernel or index its `-F` measure within its ratchets; for a gate the criteria of §2.24; the architecture section written; the two reviews (independent at a gate); the section removed |

**Kinds.**

| Kind | One step is |
| --- | --- |
| `base` | one store: its layout, its API and its `-F` measure |
| `kernel` | one algorithm over bases (a meeting, a settlement pass, a clearing) with its API and `-F` measure |
| `index` | one derived index over a base, maintained by its writer and rebuilt at load |
| `migration` | today's users of one base moved onto it, and the code it replaces deleted |
| `mechanism` | one rule or process of the spec, activating bases |
| `data` | one mapping of sources in hand into primitives, or one set of the opening's instances drawn from them |
| `tool` | one change to `phx-check`, the bench, `phx-fin` or `tools/` |
| `repair` | one defect fixed where it stands |
| `docs` | one change to the architecture, the spec or this file that no code follows in the same step |
| `gate` | a stage's judgement: the gate run and what it reads |

**The size rule.** A step is one reviewable change. A reviewer refuses a step, and it is split into several before
any code is written, when it:
- adds more than one store or kernel, or pairs a base with its migration or with behaviour on it: a `base`,
  `kernel` or `index` step that also edits `phx-world` or an older kernel crate is a base paired with its migration;
- completes more than about ten clauses. Part L's chains, read by N4's one tool, count as one clause;
- names files in more than one crate. For a `base`, `kernel` or `index` step the one crate is its kernel crate, with
  its tests, its `phx-fin` module, its data and its architecture section; the saves' base (K-104) is `phx-world`'s
  `save/` module, since a snapshot walks every crate's bases and only the assembly sees them all. For a `mechanism` or
  `data` step the one crate is a `sys-*` crate; it may also touch that system's `if-*` vocabulary module, its
  `phx-world` route, its `phx-cli` live checks, its `phx-obs` panel and a `phx-check` rule, and no other `sys-*` or
  kernel crate. Rules in two `sys-*` crates, or an edit to a kernel crate after the core, are refused outright; a
  second `sys-*` crate that only declares is split as well. Two allowances are declared: a step retires the
  placeholder it replaces in that placeholder's own crate, as part of the step; and under PC-40 a step may add the one
  lender's-value function it needs in `sys-bnk`, and no other `sys-bnk` rule;
- in Stage 8, turns more than one decision cluster (one decider, one occasion, at most three decision points) into
  options;
- holds a design one review cannot hold, or runs past about 90 lines of this file. A verbatim data block the step
  commits (the design point's figure set in `perf/design.toml`) or an inventory its base must hold whole (a code
  table, a catalogue, an instance list) does not count toward the lines: the change is sized, not the text;
- has parts (a, b, c…) or sub-steps, or files of more than one **Kind**.

### 0.3 Live checks

A live check:
- is code in `crates/apps/phx-cli/src/checks/`;
- is registered with a permanent identifier `LC-<stage>-<nn>`;
- reads a run's records, metrics and state through the inspector's read-only surface;
- returns pass, fail (with the facts that failed) or not applicable.

Every gate's run (`tools/bench.sh -g`, §2.24) runs every live check, forever. A check that stops applying is marked
`retired` with its reason; its identifier is never reused, and `phx-check` enforces both.

A live check never repairs, never writes, and never sets up the world it reads. The one exception is N1's
injection, a test of the audit and not a run of the world: `phx inject` loads a save apart, applies one audit
family's declared injection, runs the audit and discards the load without stepping a day. Its checks read the
tool's report.

**The gate run** of a stage is the bench's gate run of the gate's commit (§2.24): settled for the owner's length, run
two years with every live check, its report carrying the budget, each stage of the day's time and the macro reads,
computed from the run's public records by the read-only observer. Its numbers test the code and are never read as
the world's. Until the owner calls the device run, the budget is judged on the bench (§12).

The world runs once (spec Appendix E 36). A check reads that run and nothing else: no copy, no second seed, no other
resolution. A check about a shock or a policy change reads the run's own occurrences of it — a hazard's event, a
decision its owner took — and is not applicable until the run has one. A check still not applicable at a gate is
listed there as not yet seen, with the run's length, and never blocks the gate (spec Appendix E 39); the
mechanism's trigger and consequence are shown meanwhile by its step's unit tests. One whose conditions the run has
met without the mechanism acting is a finding.

### 0.4 Changing this plan

- Step identifiers are permanent: `S<stage>.<nn>` for the steps numbered so, `S<stage>.<nnn>` for the rest; none is
  ever renumbered or reused.
- Each stage's steps take three-digit numbers in its range (§1). As written, ids within a range increase in build
  order with no gaps, the gate last. A step inserted later takes the next free number of the range of the group it
  belongs to and goes at its dependency position; the order of steps in the file is the build order, whatever
  their numbers.
- When a step is done its whole section is removed; its rows stay in §13, and whatever needs keeping about how it
  was built is in the architecture.
- A change to the design of a done step is a new step that says what it changes and why.
- A step that will never be built is `retired` and moves to §11, keeping its heading and its **Status** with its
  reason or the steps its work went to. It holds no row of §13.
- A step's rows in §13 are written, moved or removed in the same commit as its heading.

### 0.5 Findings

A finding — a failing live check, an audit family that fires, a number that looks wrong, a mechanism that never
runs, a measure that misses, a reviewer's finding — is a finding about a missing or wrong mechanism, and it is solved
at once, in the step where it is found, however long or complicated. There is no findings table and no finding
identifier. What truly cannot be settled now — an owner decision, or a mechanism of a later step — is written into
the step that will settle it: its design takes the work, with what was measured and where, and its **Done when** the
check. Nothing is tuned to make a finding go away (spec N7, GEN.11), and no bound is added to stop a number
exploding: the mechanism that holds it is built (Law 6). A state that cannot exist — a one-sided flow, a negative
count of units, a fact with two writers — is fixed where it is.

### 0.6 Owner decisions

The owner's decisions are those the spec reserves: the open items of Appendix E, the performance budget (N8), the
order in which the resolution is refined (N8.5), the save time (N8.10), the settling length (GEN.6) and the size of
the map. They are recorded in §12 with the answer and its date. A step that needs one not yet recorded stops and
asks. Every other question is derived from the spec and the laws, and the answer is stated in the commit.

### 0.7 The review prompts

**Reviewer A (spec and laws)**

> Read `CLAUDE.md`, the step's section in `docs/IMPLEMENTATION.md`, the spec clauses it lists and the laws
> (spec Part I). Then read the diff (`git diff <base>..HEAD`).
>
> For each clause, say where the diff carries it and whether it carries it exactly. Look for:
> - an outcome written as a rule;
> - a default standing in for a missing value, or an absent value read as zero;
> - a bound;
> - a kind branch;
> - a second writer or a second representation;
> - a read of the future or of another party's private state;
> - a draw outside a named stream;
> - a one-sided flow;
> - a number that is not a register entry;
> - a mechanism the spec does not state, or states otherwise;
> - anything the change needs that the spec does not say, without the spec amended in its own commit.
>
> Report blockers, serious and minor findings, each with file and line, the clause it breaks and a one-line fix.
> Change nothing.

**Reviewer B (architecture, budget and shortcuts)**

> Read `CLAUDE.md`, the step's section in `docs/IMPLEMENTATION.md`, the architecture sections it lists, §2.22 and
> §2.23 of the plan, and the step's **Not allowed**. Then read the diff.
>
> Look for:
> - departures from the step's types, layouts and algorithms;
> - layering and channel breaches;
> - a store, index, map or per-party pass outside the core bases, in a `sys-*` crate or in `phx-world`;
> - a change to a base's layout outside that base's own step, or data a base reads declared other than through its
>   extension points;
> - a pass over every party every day: anything not due-driven, event-driven or a declared rolling slice;
> - an allocation per day: a buffer not kept across days, a collection built or cloned on a day's path;
> - hidden full sweeps, maps or trait objects on a day's path, serial work that should be sharded;
> - unmeasured costs and counters not ratcheted;
> - for a base, kernel or index: its `tools/bench.sh -F <base>` measure at the design point, for B, NB and H days,
>   within its `[fin.<base>]` ratchets, and extension points that cover every later clause that reads or writes it;
> - each edge case E1–E14 (plan §2.23) that applies, answered by a named unit test or live check;
> - tests that build a world, and live checks that set up what they read;
> - comments that reference documents, clauses or history;
> - a decision the change takes that `docs/ARCHITECTURE.md` or this plan does not yet say, or now contradicts.
>
> Run the step's budget measurements yourself: `tools/bench.sh` at the committed resolution, and `-F <base>` for a
> base. Report as Reviewer A does. Change nothing.

## 1. The build at a glance

Stages follow spec Part O, in the order below: Stage 8, the minds, is built after Stage 3 and keeps its number,
since identifiers are permanent. Each stage ends with its gate step, where its exit and the budget (N8) are judged on
the settled run, and from Stage 1 its macro reads are reported against real economies' (spec Appendix E 25). Every
base the finished world needs is built in Stage 1's core, before any behaviour is put on it; every later step
activates bases.

| Stage | Range | What it holds |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **0 Foundations** | S0.01–S0.28 | done: the workspace, the foundation and kernel crates, the map, the setup and the persistence |
| **1 The circular flow**, done | S1.01–S1.14, S1.17–S1.23, S1.26 | done: the Stage 1 systems' declarations and rules, the meter, one representation, the core and the bench, money and settlement, markets and goods on the core, one opening dataset per profile, Stage 0's world on the core, the decision core |
| **1 The core: frame and tools** | none (S1.100–S1.133 done) | the architecture's frame at the design point; the finished-volume measure (`tools/bench.sh -F`, `phx-fin`); `perf/design.toml`; `phx-check`'s rules for bases and steps; the ratchets |
| **1 The core: what the bases stand on** | none (S1.137, S1.141–S1.146, S1.152, S1.153, S1.156 done) | the repairs a base depends on, built first: kinds' declared features, handles bound at assembly, the pool in settlement and the wheel takes, one decision runtime |
| **1 The core: bases** | S1.163–S1.360 (S1.159–S1.162 done) | every store, kernel and index the finished world needs, each designed for its last user and measured at the design point, each followed by the migration of its current users |
| **1 The core: repairs** | S1.135–S1.158 but those above, S1.361 (S1.134 done) | defects that stand apart from any base, repaired after the bases where a base has not already fixed them |
| **1 Stage 1 on the core** | S1.400–S1.499 | Stage 0's and Stage 1's mechanisms as rules over the bases, Stage 1's remaining clauses, the opening's derivations, and the Stage 1 gate |
| **2 Credit and failure** | S2.100–S2.216 | losses and provisions, trade credit, the firm's lifecycle, estates in kind, housing and places, bank funding, capital and supervision, energy, the credit bureau and filed accounts, personal insolvency; the gate |
| **3 Money and capital markets** | S3.100–S3.219 | the money market, the central bank and the treasury in full, sovereign and corporate debt, equity, dealers, funds, non-bank lenders, indices, ratings; the gate |
| **8 Minds** (built after Stage 3) | S8.100–S8.202 | the mind kernel's rules, characters, households' and offices' minds, experience, aspirations and learning, the life record; the gate |
| **4 Risk transfer** | S4.100–S4.185 | derivatives and their classes, insurance, pensions, securitisation, takeovers; the gate |
| **5 The full state and the open world** | S5.100–S5.187 | taxes and social protection in full, politics, currencies, trade, finance and migration across borders; the gate |
| **6 Growth and the full population** | S6.100–S6.142 | technology, demography and households in full, the observer and the app in full, the opening and the audit complete; the gate |
| **7 Realism** | S7.100–S7.106 | the stylised facts, the chain relationships, calibration; the realism gate |

## 2. Conventions every step follows

These are decisions taken once, so that fifty systems written over years read as one codebase. A step may not depart
from them. A convention changes only by a change to this section, in its own commit, with its reason.

### 2.1 Repository layout

```text
crates/foundation/{phx-macros,phx-num,phx-rand,phx-id}/
crates/kernel/                  the kernels and the core's bases, in layering order (each depends only on those
                                before it); a new crate is created by the step named
  phx-store                     tables, generation references, day buffers, indexes, rings, saves' columns
  phx-exec                      the pool, chunk plans, partitioned apply, sweeps, the trace and counters
  phx-core                      declarations, the register, kinds, the calendar, units, the stage
                                table, capacities, findings
  phx-geo                       the map, places, cells, networks and routes, deposits, weather
  phx-pop                       parties of every kind, persons, offices, the per-day party cache
  phx-record                    events, records by vintage, the day ledger, statistics, life records (S1.212)
  phx-agenda                    the due wheel, the decision agenda, hazards drawn ahead, messages, triggers (S1.225)
  phx-ledger                    money accounts, flows, settlement, commitments, levies, tallies
  phx-contract                  contracts between named parties: families, sides, terms, status, books (S1.257)
  phx-hold                      holdings of goods, units and instruments, lots, bounds, capital, processes (S1.271)
  phx-market                    standing offers and every market form, the sales batch, prints and marks
  phx-acct                      account lines, equity, carrying values, statements
  phx-val                       valuations, curves, public series and outlooks
  phx-risk                      books and limits, netting, margin and collateral, linear aggregates (S1.338)
  phx-end                       estates, endings, claims and the waterfall, resolution (S1.342)
  phx-mind                      the decision core, attention, minds (S1.348)
  phx-audit                     the audit engine and injection (S1.353)
crates/interfaces/if-*/         shared vocabulary between systems
crates/systems/sys-*/           each system's declarations and rules
crates/assembly/{phx-world,phx-obs}/   the assembly and the day's routing; the read-only observer
crates/apps/{phx-cli,phx-check,phx-fin}/   the run, `inject`, `fin` and live checks; the drift guards; the
                                finished-volume measure, one module per base (S1.116; L0 and kernel crates only)
android/                        the Compose app
data/world.toml                 the calendar's constants and the world's units
data/shared/<SYS>.toml          primitives common to all countries; `GEN.toml` holds the generator's world constants
                                (the population, the countries and regions, the map's size, the settling length),
                                `SET.toml` the save interval, `SHAPES.toml` every standing rule form
data/setup/default.toml         the default new game: the population split and each country's choices and name
data/profiles/<level>/{economy,people,law,profile}.toml   a development level's four files: its accounts, its
                                people, its law, and the joint draw of a country's derived values (GEN.15)
data/profiles/<level>/later/<SYS>.toml   tables of a system a later stage builds, taken only with it
data/sources/raw/               every published series in hand, with its `manifest.json`
data/inventory.toml             the opening's inventory: every derived value, its owner, its first reader, its source
data/measure/                   the realism reads' definitions (N3, N4)
data/observer/READS.toml        the observer's macro reads
data/names/                     real institution and currency names, and the name generator's lists
data/<country>/                 one country's primitives, instantiated at a new game; never committed
perf/budget.toml                the budget's ratchets at the committed resolution, and each base's `[fin.<base>]`
                                ratchets at the design point
perf/ratchets.toml              counter ratchets (§2.11)
perf/design.toml                the design point: counts, daily volumes, the phone model, the RESOLUTION settings it
                                is measured at (§2.11); the world never reads it
perf/bench/                     the bench's kept reports (`tools/bench.sh -k`)
perf/reads/                     each gate's macro reads from its run (§2.24)
tools/bench.sh                  the bench, the one tool that runs and measures the world (§2.10)
tools/data/                     the derivations from `data/sources/raw/` into primitives, and `profile_files.py`
tools/versions.toml             the pinned tool versions
docs/                           the spec, the architecture, this file
```

A step's **Files** row naming a country's primitives commits them into its level's four files, each in the one that
describes it, written by id through `tools/data/profile_files.py`, one per development level, with their sources; a
table that repeats a fact another holds is derived from it, not stored. A system a later stage builds keeps its
tables in `later/<SYS>.toml` until it is built: a new game copies them only for a system the world keeps, since the
register refuses an entry no system declares. `perf/` is reviewed by the owner (`CODEOWNERS`).

### 2.2 Inside a crate

- `src/lib.rs` holds module declarations and re-exports, and in a system crate the system's type and its
  declarations.
- `src/consts.rs` holds engineering constants (chunk sizes, thresholds between exact algorithms, buffer horizons),
  one `pub const` each with a comment saying why its value is what it is (§2.18). No other file has a numeric literal
  other than 0, 1, −1 or 2 (§2.7).
- **Kernel crates** hold the bases: each base's store, its API — batch entry points for a day's items, views a rule
  reads, writes by its one writer — and its tests. A per-party mutator is not public to world code.
- **System crates** hold rules and declarations only, never a store, a handler, a day buffer or a loop over parties:

  | File | Contents |
  | --- | --- |
  | `src/lib.rs` | the zero-sized system type and its `System::declare`: every declaration, as data a base reads (a kind's record words, contract families and their shapes, flow reasons, record kinds and series, streams, primitives, audit families, metrics) |
  | `src/points.rs` | its decision points (`DecisionPointDecl`), each with its rule, its schedule or wakes and its clause |
  | `src/rules/<decision>.rs` | the pure rule functions, one per decision, each its own evaluation form |
  | `src/opening.rs` | its contributions to the opening, as pure functions over what the opening's base hands them |
  | `src/<concept>.rs` | other pure functions and declared tables its rules read (a law's schedule, a kind's table) |

- **`phx-world`** assembles the bases and the systems' declarations and routes the day: at each stage of the day it
  calls the bases' entry points and hands the rules their views. It holds no store and no per-party pass; a
  `core_*` module that holds one is moved into its base by that base's migration step, and none is added.
- **`phx-fin`** holds one module per base, `src/<base>.rs`, implementing its driver: it fills that base with seeded
  random data at `perf/design.toml`'s volumes and runs its entry points at the design point's daily counts. It
  depends on foundation and kernel crates only, never a system or `phx-world`, and `phx fin` (`tools/bench.sh -F`)
  runs it.
- **Interface crates** have one module per concept and no function bodies beyond constructors and field accessors
  (PC-08).
- **Files tables**: a row whose path starts `src/` belongs to the crate of the nearest full path above it, or, with
  none above, to the step's own crate.

### 2.3 Names

| Thing | Form | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| System code | the spec's code | `LAB` |
| Primitive | `<SYS>.<snake_case>` | `DEM.mortality_table` |
| Decision point | `<SYS>.<snake_case>` | `FRM.produce` |
| Stream | `<SYS>.<process>` | `DEM.mortality` |
| Metric | `<SYS>.<snake_case>` | `LAB.vacancies_open` |
| Audit family | `<SYS>.<family>` | `MON.issuer_balance` |
| Span of the day | `<stage>.<what>` | `settle.fixed_point` |
| Live check | `LC-<stage>-<nn>` | `LC-1-21` |
| `phx-check` rule | `PC-<nn>` | `PC-92` |
| Counter | `<crate>.<snake_case>` | `phx_core.flows_a_day` |
| Base ratchet | `fin.<base>.<measure>` | `fin.retail.match_ns` |
| Step | `S<stage>.<nnn>` | `S1.159` |

Types are nouns in the spec's words (`EmploymentContract`, not `EmpCtr`). No abbreviation that the spec's glossary
does not use.

### 2.4 Clauses in code

- The item that **carries** a clause bears `#[clause("REP.8")]`:
  - a type or store for STATE;
  - a decision point's rule function for DECISION;
  - the function that runs the process — a base's entry point or the routing that calls a rule — for PROCESS;
  - an audit family for INVARIANT;
  - a metric for MEASURE;
  - a check, clippy rule or refusing type for FORBID;
  - a register entry for PRIMITIVE.
- Declarations carry the clause as data (a `clause` field), and so do data files (a `clause` key).
- `phx-check clauses` verifies that each clause a done step completes has a carrier: a `#[clause(..)]` attribute, a
  declaration's `clause` field, a data file's `clause` key or a contract's `violation!(clause = ..)` (architecture
  §16.5). The carrier's shape is not checked.
- Comments never name clauses, documents or history. The attribute is the only link.

### 2.5 Violations and findings

- A **contract violation** is an impossible state (II.5). It is raised at its site by `violation!(clause = "SET.4",
  "what is impossible", key = value, …)`, defined in `phx-num`, the lowest crate every other depends on.
  - It never returns and nothing catches it. With `panic = "abort"`, the application's panic hook writes
    `violations/<run-id>.json` and aborts.
  - The report carries the clause, the message and the keys, and the site — the day, the stage of the day and its
    span, the chunk — which `phx-exec` records per thread in its one named thread-local. Code outside any recorded
    site reports it as `outside`.
  - `clause` may name a clause (`SET.4`) or a law (`Law 7`).
- An **engineering limit** reached — a reservation, a field width, an index size — is not a clause of the world. It
  is raised by `capacity_exceeded!(what, declared, needed)`, which names the declaration to enlarge, and it also
  stops the run.
- An **audit finding** is an invariant broken. It is recorded in the run's findings, kept outside the world's hash:
  `Finding { family, clause, owner, size: i128, unit, day, detail }`, the owner a party, tile, contract, instrument,
  market or country, the unit `Money(Ccy)` or `Qty(UnitId)`. The audit never repairs (N1, Law 17).
- A **run finding** — a live check that fails, a measure outside its expected range — is solved at once (§0.5). The
  run's report lists every audit finding and every failing live check.

### 2.6 Numbers and data

- Every declared number is a register entry in `data/`, with its kind, unit and owner (NUM.3), in this form. A key
  that does not apply is **absent**, never empty:

  ```toml
  [[primitive]]
  id = "DEM.mortality_table"
  kind = "TECHNOLOGY"          # TECHNOLOGY | PREFERENCE | POLICY | ENDOWMENT | RESOLUTION | SHAPE
  unit = "per person per year"
  period = "year"              # only for rates and flows
  owner = "DEM"                # the system that reads and declares it
  decided_by = "treasury"      # POLICY only: the institution's role that may change it (Law 2, Law 16)
  source = "measured"          # measured | estimated | assumed | placeholder
  source_ref = "…"             # a citation, or the reason for an assumption
  shape = "placeholder:LAB"    # SHAPE only: "placeholder:<SYS>" or "standing:<reason>"
  value = …                    # scalar, table or distribution, typed by the declaration
  ```

- A system reads a primitive only through the typed handle its declaration returns. Assembly refuses an entry with
  no declaration, and a declaration with no entry.
- **The data are in hand.** Every published series a step reads is already in `data/sources/raw/`, listed in its
  `manifest.json` with the steps that read it (`for`) and, when derived, typed from a paper or simulated, how
  (`note`). A step maps those series into its primitives with a derivation under `tools/data/` and adds its rows to
  `data/inventory.toml`; it never searches for data. What no source gives is derived from those that do, taken from
  a paper's table or simulated by a declared procedure, and said so.
- **Missing is missing.** An absent value is `Missing::Absent` or a refusal, never a default and never zero.
- **State holds no floating-point number.** Money and units are `i64`, and rates and positions are fixed-point `i64`
  in declared units; `i128` only for world totals. Floats exist only inside pure functions (§2.19).
- **No `min`, `max` or `clamp` on a number the world decides** (Law 6). Three typed operations replace them:
  - `Qty::matched(offered, wanted)`, the quantity both sides of a trade accept;
  - `Day::earlier` and `Day::later`;
  - `DeclaredLimit::bind`, for a real limit.

  Any other use needs `#[expect(clippy::disallowed_methods, reason = "…")]`, and the count of those only falls.

### 2.7 Literals

Mechanism code contains no numeric literal other than 0, 1, −1 and 2 (PC-06).
- Literals in **type positions** (array lengths, const-generic arguments) are allowed, since they state a layout, not
  a number of the world. Shift counts and bit widths use named constants or `u32::BITS` and its kin.
- Mathematical constants of an algorithm (Philox multipliers, the BTPE switch point) live in `consts.rs` with their
  source.
- `tests/`, `benches/` and `#[cfg(test)]` code are exempt, and so is `phx-fin`, which is no mechanism: its fill
  shapes are its own constants in `src/fill.rs`, and its volumes come from `perf/design.toml`.

### 2.8 Mechanisms

A mechanism is a pure rule over a view a base builds, taken through the decision core and written back through a
base's API:

```rust
// sys-frm/src/points.rs
pub const PRODUCE: DecisionPointDecl<ProduceIn, Produce> = DecisionPointDecl {
    name: "FRM.produce", system: "FRM", rule: target,
    schedule: Missing::Present("FRM.production_days"), wakes: &[], runs_on_non_business: false, clause: "FRM.4",
};

// sys-frm/src/rules/produce.rs
#[clause("FRM.4")]
pub fn target(input: &ProduceIn) -> Produce { … }
```

- **Inputs** are a typed view the base fills from its columns for the party the decision is due for: the party's
  own state, public records after their lag, and what it bought or was sent (Law 12). A rule never reaches a store.
- **When it runs**: on its schedule (a due on the base's wheel), on a declared wake (a trigger tested where the fact
  is written, at O(1) a write), or at an occasion; never by a look at every party.
- **Who decides**: `Core::decide` names the decider — the player, an office's holder, founding preferences, a
  household or a person — as `MND.decisions` declares the point, and counts the decision.
- **Outputs** are written through the base's API by its one writer, or emitted as flows under a declared reason;
  levies arise with their base flow.
- A mechanism allocates nothing per row or per day; its scratch is a day buffer the base owns, kept across days.

### 2.9 Logic-level tests

- Tests live in `#[cfg(test)] mod tests` beside the code (or a `<module>_tests.rs` file beside it), named
  `<subject>_<what_holds>`, and use only values they build themselves: numbers, small slices, pure functions.
- A test never constructs a `World`, a `Registry` or a store of the real world. A test that needs a table builds a
  `phx-store` column over a `HeapBacking`; that is data, not a world. A kernel's hand-built fixture of a few parties,
  contracts and accounts, asserting that kernel's own arithmetic, is a logic-level test (§12).
- **Statistical tests** of samplers use fixed keys. Their thresholds are normal bounds at z ≥ 6.1 (a false-failure
  probability below 10⁻⁹), derived in the test's comment, so the tests are deterministic. A key is never changed to
  make a test pass: a failure is a defect in the sampler or the test's derivation.
- `proptest` is allowed as a dev-dependency, with a fixed seed and case count from `consts.rs`, reduced under
  `cfg(miri)`.
- `trybuild` compile-fail tests prove what the types refuse.
- `phx-fin`'s fill is a measure, not a test: it asserts nothing about the world.

### 2.10 Live checks and the bench

```rust
pub const LC_1_21: Check = live_check! {
    id: "LC-1-21",
    title: "…",
    from_step: "S1.08",
    check: jobs_are_filled,          // fn(Inspector<'_>) -> Outcome
};
```

- `Inspector` is the read-only surface of `phx-world`. It has no method that writes, and PC-20 refuses a `&mut`
  reaching the world from `checks/`.
- A check reads only what the run left: records, metrics, findings, state at a close.
- **The bench** (`tools/bench.sh`) is the one tool that runs and measures the world, on the build machine (the
  development VM, architecture §14.7). Its flags set the persons (`-p`), days (`-d`), seed (`-s`), workers (`-w`),
  live checks (`-c`), a time limit (`-t`) and a sampling profile (`-P`); `-g` is a gate's run, `-k` keeps the report
  in `perf/bench/`, `-F <base,…|all>` is the finished-volume measure (`phx fin`, §2.22) and `-D` picks its day types
  and turns (`B`, `NB`, `H`, `BC`, `turn`). The run's trace streams every
  span of the opening and the day with its time and notes, and the bench writes the run's whole report — each day's
  stages and their time, the budget, memory, cores, the flows, the findings and the checks — and a summary. CI builds
  and runs the tests and `phx-check`, never the world.
- **Every step** runs the bench at the committed resolution for 20 days from day zero, the budget's ratchets
  (`perf/budget.toml`) read against it; a step does not end with one broken unless it says why.
- **A base, kernel or index** also runs `tools/bench.sh -F <base>` at the design point (§2.22).
- **A stage gate** runs `tools/bench.sh -g` and `-F all` and is judged by §2.24.
- The play resolution is a declared RESOLUTION setting (`REP.persons`), changed only by a recorded change between
  runs, never by in-run timing, citing a report the bench kept (`-k`). A run at fewer persons (`-p`) is for speed,
  for that run only. Nothing runs the world twice, not even to prove determinism.

### 2.11 Counters, ratchets and the budget frame

- The bench counts, per span, the items, CPU ns summed over threads, wall ns, allocations, page faults and rows
  visited; the core counts flows, dues, decisions, rounds, bytes a person and faults a day.
- CI's wall time is never ratcheted. The bench's is, in `perf/budget.toml`: the turn's median and worst, bytes a
  person, faults a day and cores busy at the committed resolution; and each base's `[fin.<base>]` ratchets at the
  design point — its unit cost in VM ns on B, NB and H days, bytes a row and MB at the design point.
- `perf/ratchets.toml` holds each counter's value and direction:

  ```toml
  [[ratchet]]
  counter = "phx_core.flows_a_day"
  value = 1376923
  direction = "down"
  ```

- A counter with no entry is refused, never read as zero (NUM.8), and one that moves the wrong way fails the run.
- A ratchet may worsen only in a commit that edits its entry, with the reason, reviewed by the owner (`CODEOWNERS`).
- **The budget frame.** `perf/design.toml` holds the one figure set of the design point — its counts (`[point]`,
  `[store]`), its daily volumes (`[day.b]`, `[day.nb]`, `[day.h]`, `[day.bc]`), the phone model (`[phone]`: the
  sustained cores and the factor k between a phone's and this machine's ns, for compute and for gathers) and the
  RESOLUTION settings it is measured at (`[resolution]`, each forced change with its `forced_by`). `perf/budget.toml`
  holds the targets: each day type's core-ms (`[fin.day]`), the turn's median and worst (`[fin.turn]`), resident
  memory (`[fin.mem]`), saves (`[fin.save]`), each base's `[fin.<base>]` and each stage line's shares (`[fin.decide]`,
  `[fin.fixed]`). A day's wall time is its core time over the phone's sustained cores; the day types' targets are
  set so that the worst calendar turn holds N8.2 with 10% headroom. Every step cites these keys and never restates
  their numbers; each per-item line carries a miss budget.
- **The steps' figures and the design point.** A step states its volumes, counts, shares, calendar and event
  core-ms, MB and MB-denominated ratchets at the counts of 7.5 million persons (`[point] steps_persons`); the design
  point is 6.0 million (spec Appendix E 51, §12), so `perf/design.toml` holds its counts and every total at 0.8 of
  the steps' statements (`[point] scale`), except what does not grow with the persons: the barriers, the process, the
  institutions, the map and network, the save buffers and the parts that follow the zones or the segments. Unit
  costs (ns an item or a row) and bytes a row are the same at either. S1.132 seeds a count's or a total's ratchet at
  the scaled figure, and `-F` measures the real ones at the design point's counts.

### 2.12 Dependencies

`phx-check` holds the external allow-list of **direct** dependencies (PC-02); transitive ones are the direct ones'
business. Each crate is allowed only in the crates named.

| Crate | Allowed in |
| --- | --- |
| `hashbrown`, `foldhash` | `phx-core`, `phx-store` |
| `libm` | foundation, kernel, systems |
| `rayon-core` | `phx-exec` |
| `libc` | `phx-exec`, `phx-store` |
| `zstd` | `phx-store` |
| `serde`, `toml` | `phx-core` (register loading), `phx-world`, `phx-obs`, `phx-cli`, `phx-check`, `phx-fin` |
| `serde_json` | `phx-cli`, `phx-check`, `phx-world` (reports), `phx-fin` |
| `clap` | `phx-cli`, `phx-check` |
| `regex` | `phx-check` |
| `syn`, `quote`, `proc-macro2` | `phx-macros`, `phx-check` |
| `cargo_metadata` | `phx-check` |
| `proptest`, `trybuild` | dev-dependencies anywhere |

Random-number crates (`rand`, `rand_core`, `getrandom`) and other hashers (`ahash`, `fxhash`) are refused as direct
dependencies of world crates (PC-13). Adding a crate or an allowed place is a change to this table, to
`phx-check`'s list and to the architecture's decision record, in its own commit.

### 2.13 Arithmetic

- Every profile builds with `overflow-checks = true`, so an integer overflow anywhere stops the run.
- Money, quantities and counts use the checked operations of `phx-num`. An overflow is `violation!(clause = "Law 7")`,
  since the exact identity can no longer hold.
- Modular (wrapping) arithmetic is allowed only where the algorithm is modular — Philox, hashing, radix digits,
  encoding deltas — through the named helpers of `phx-rand`, `phx-store` and `phx-exec`. `wrapping_*`,
  `saturating_*` and `overflowing_*` are refused everywhere else (clippy lists).

### 2.14 Errors

- `Result` is for a refusal the caller must handle as part of the world: a payment fails, an order has no match, a
  register entry is malformed at assembly.
- `violation!` is for a state that cannot exist: a currency mixed, units negative, a fact with two writers.
- A pure function returns `Result` only for input it can meet in a legal world. Otherwise it violates.

### 2.15 Rounding

A `Round` is always read from a declared convention — a contract's terms, a law, a unit's declaration. It is never
written as a literal in a mechanism. `Round::InFavourOf(Side)` expresses "in the payee's favour" (MON.16).

### 2.16 Chance

- Each process has its own stream (`<SYS>.<process>`), declared with its purpose.
- Draws are made only through the streams the core opens (`phx_core::streams`; PC-19). A draw's address is (stream,
  subject, day, block), so no result depends on the order draws are made in. The subject is the thing acted on: a
  party, a contract, a tile, a region, a zone, a country, a market, an instrument, or the world.
- A (stream, subject) is opened at most once a day for its purpose; a second open would repeat its draws, a
  violation of CHN.6.
- Never a clock, never unseeded randomness, never iteration order.

### 2.17 Order

- No result depends on the order of anything unordered (CHN.6). No map or trait object sits on a day's path (PC-92);
  a map elsewhere is read in sorted order, never in storage order.
- Every ordered output — a gather, a list, a tie — is ordered by permanent identity (party, contract, instrument),
  then by declared rule, and ties a rule leaves equal go by lot (CHN.3).
- Slot order is storage, never an order of outcomes. Work is chunked by rows and declared costs, never by the
  number of workers, and joined in chunk order, so the result is the same for any number of workers. Any id a pass
  assigns — an event, a message, a contract created at a split, a new party — is assigned after its items are
  ordered by (the subject's permanent identity, the subject's own sequence), and every sort whose ties would fall back
  on input order carries those two as its last keys.

### 2.18 Constants

`consts.rs` holds engineering constants only: chunk sizes, thresholds for switching between exact algorithms,
buffer growth, horizons of in-memory buffers. None may change the distribution of any outcome of the world. A
constant that would is a primitive.

### 2.19 Floats

- Floats appear only inside pure functions.
- Uniforms lie on the **open** interval (0, 1), as (k + ½)·2⁻⁵² for a 52-bit k: at 53 bits the largest value,
  (2⁵³ − ½)·2⁻⁵³, rounds to 1.
- Transcendental functions come from `libm`; `mul_add` and platform intrinsics are refused.
- Small probabilities use `log1p` and `expm1`.
- An `f64` becomes an integer only by checked rounding, which refuses a non-finite or out-of-range value (NUM.6).

### 2.20 Encoding, diagnostics and names

- Everything saved or hashed is **little-endian**.
- World crates print nothing (`println!` and its kin are refused). They report through records, metrics, spans and
  findings, and only the applications print.
- Field names carry their unit or period when a type does not: `_days`, `_m` (metres), `_per_year`, `_ppm`.

### 2.21 Decisions and behaviour

The spec states each decision's inputs, never its answer (Part II). A rule's **form** is a design decision taken here,
grounded in the literature it names. **Every** decision rule's form is a standing SHAPE (spec Law 2 and Appendix C):
it is listed in `data/shared/SHAPES.toml` with its reason — no mechanism in scope derives how people decide — and its
source, and `phx-check` refuses a decision point whose form is not listed. Its **parameters** are primitives
(PREFERENCE, TECHNOLOGY or POLICY) in the register, with sources; no parameter is an outcome (a markup, a propensity
to consume, a default probability), which is either a position the party carries and updates or a read. Every rule is
a pure function, and is its own evaluation form (REP.15).

- **Inputs are the spec's.** A rule reads every input its DECISION clause lists, and nothing a party could not know:
  its own state, public records after their lag, and what it bought or was sent (Law 12).
- **Every decision goes through the decision core**, its decider named, in the office or standing `MND.decisions`
  declares for it (§2.8). A decision a step adds after Stage 8 is written as its options and their consequences by
  concern, which the deciding mind weighs (MND).
- **When a DECISION clause is complete.** A DECISION built whole as a rule through the decision core, from exactly
  the inputs its clause lists, completes its clause; Stage 8's turning it into options is MND.7's work and cites the
  clause in **Design** without moving it. A step that builds as a fixed formula what its clause says is chosen is
  wrong, and is fixed to build the choice (§12).
- **Reviewing costs something real** (REP.21, Law 14). Each lumpy decision's review cost is TECHNOLOGY in hours: a
  firm's come out of its staff's hours that day (so review is paid in capacity), a household's out of its adults'
  leisure (so it enters the value of leisure its next decisions read). A menu cost of changing a posted point is paid
  the same way. The cost is counted per decision kind.
- **No kind branches** (Law 10): what differs between kinds is declared data a rule reads.
- **Streams** are named `<SYS>.<process>` in each step, one per purpose (§2.16).
- **Counters** named in each step are ratcheted in `perf/ratchets.toml` or `perf/budget.toml` (§2.11).
- **Interface crates** follow the architecture's layer order, with shared identifiers in `if-base`.
- **Unit tests** are pure functions over values they are handed, or compile-level refusals (§2.9); anything that needs
  a registry or a world is a live check.
- **Placeholders** name the system and step that retire them; each retiring step says so.

### 2.22 Bases and activation

**A base step** (`base`, `kernel` or `index`) delivers, in one crate:
- **the store or kernel**: its layout as fixed-stride columns by slot, hot words apart from cold, with its capacity
  declared for the design point and its growth over two years; small per-party collections inline with a declared
  capacity and an overflow column; adjacency only as the edge tables' threading;
- **its API**: batch entry points for a day's items, typed views a rule reads, writes by its one writer, its
  maintained aggregates (integers, `#[maintained(writer = …)]`), its save (`#[saved(skip, rebuild = …)]` for every
  derived index) and its extension points;
- **its `phx-fin` module**: the base filled with seeded random data at its size at the design point and run through
  its entry points at the design point's daily counts on B, NB and H days;
- **its architecture section**: volumes, access pattern, unit cost, miss budget, memory, traversal and extension
  points;
- **its ratchets**: `perf/budget.toml [fin.<base>]`, and the `phx-check` guards that hold its discipline.

Its migration — today's users moved onto it, in `phx-world` or an older kernel, and the code it replaces deleted —
is its own step, right after it; a base step never also migrates.

The core's design rules bind every base, each a `phx-check` rule or a ratchet where it can be: columns per kind,
dense by slot, no maps, lists or wide optionals on a day's path; due-driven traversal, nothing visiting every party
every day, a world-sized pass only as a declared rolling slice; decide, then apply by party range, the same result
for any number of workers; maintained aggregates the audit never reads, the audit recounting from source rows; no
allocation in the day, every day buffer owned by its base, sized by the heaviest day and kept; per-item effects
batched and partitioned by target; per-day values computed once; one dispatch a pass over cost-sized chunks; saves
of live rows with every index rebuilt at load; every span counted; O(log n) per operation in the size of any store;
a miss budget per item.

**An activation step** (`mechanism`, `data`) may:
- add rules under `sys-*/src/rules/` and decision points in `points.rs`;
- declare data a base reads, through that base's extension point: a kind's record words, a contract family and its
  shape, a flow reason, a record kind with its audience and horizon, a public series, a due's schedule or a wake, a
  primitive;
- declare an instance of a core index, or a sweep of a core base, through its extension point, with its line in
  ARCHITECTURE §13's ledger (bytes and time) and its E6 treatment (saved, or rebuilt at load with the load's cost);
- route in `phx-world`: at a stage of the day, call a base's entry point and hand a rule its view;
- map data in hand into primitives, and add live checks and the observer's panel for what it adds.

It may not add a store, index, map, kernel, day buffer, dispatch or per-party pass; change a base's layout; call a
per-party mutator in a loop over a day's items; or read a store other than through a base's view.

**Declared data.** A system declares what a base reads in `System::declare`, in the declaration types the base
exposes; assembly validates each against the base (a missing field, an unknown reason, an office no form declares is
refused) and each base sizes itself from the declarations at assembly. A need no declaration covers is a new base
step before the step that needs it (§0.1 rule 5).

### 2.23 Edge cases

Each step's **Edge cases** lists the cases that apply to it and how it meets each. By default:

| Id | Case | Answered by |
| --- | --- | --- |
| E1 | Mass failure on one day: a bank, a tenth of the firms, a region struck | endings are events handled by the estates' base at a cost per ending; the heavy day in `-F` carries an ending wave; the gate's run reads the day of most endings within the budget |
| E2 | An empty market: no seller, no buyer, one side only | the kernel returns no match, never divides by zero; a price not formed stays missing; a unit test for each side empty |
| E3 | A party with nothing: no account, holding or contract, unbanked | every API accepts the empty party; a payment to or from a party with no money fails as `NoMoney` and stays in arrears (MON.12); a unit test |
| E4 | Estates that never liquidate | an estate stays open, holding its claims and contracts, until its assets are sold or its claims met; nothing closes it by a bound; its storage is counted in the base's growth; a live check counts estates open |
| E5 | Heavy days: month- and quarter-end paydays after closed days, filing windows, elections, busy market days | buffers sized by the heaviest day; the `-F` H profile and its ratchets; the worst turn read at the gate |
| E6 | Save and load mid-run | saved state is live rows only; every derived index is rebuilt at load in canonical order and the logical hash is equal; a unit test that a rebuilt index equals the maintained one; the gate's save check |
| E7 | Any number of workers | chunks by rows and declared costs, draws by address, apply by party range, joins in chunk order; a kernel's unit test over a fixture at one and several workers |
| E8 | Capacity and overflow: ids, counts, money in `i64`/`i128`, a store's growth | checked arithmetic; widths declared for the design point with two years' growth; `capacity_exceeded!` naming the declaration; a unit test at the boundary |
| E9 | Growth over a two-year run within declared horizons (SET.12–SET.16) | every record and store states its horizon and growth; what passes its horizon is released at the close; `-F` fills two years' growth; bytes ratcheted |
| E10 | A party ending while contracts, holdings, offices, orders or indices point at it | references carry a generation and `resolve` refuses a stale one; slots are released only after the close; what points at it moves to its estate or ends by an event; a unit test of the stale reference |
| E11 | The first day and day zero: nothing yet recorded | no history is missing, never zero; each rule states what it reads on day zero; a unit test |
| E12 | Missing data | an absent value stays absent: a refusal at assembly or a named `Missing`, never 0; a unit test of the refusal |
| E13 | A currency, country or kind with none of something | an empty set does no work and divides by nothing; a unit test with the set empty |
| E14 | Simultaneous events on one party the same day | effects accumulate in nets and commute; ties go by identity, then rule, then lot; a unit test permuting the input order |

### 2.24 The gate

Every stage ends with its gate step, of Kind `gate`, a major step. Its **Design** cites this section and adds only
its stage's own heavy days, macro reads and exit checks; nothing here is restated in a gate.

- **The run**: `tools/bench.sh -g` at the committed resolution — settled for the owner's length (§12), run two
  years, the audit every day, every live check, a save and a load mid-run with the logical hash equal — and
  `tools/bench.sh -F all -D B,NB,H,BC,turn` at the design point. Both reports are kept (`-k`, `perf/bench/`), and
  the macro reads computed from the run's public records by the read-only observer are written to
  `perf/reads/<gate id>-*.json`.
- **Pass criteria**, read from §12 and `perf/budget.toml`, never written as literals:
  - **time** (N8.2): at the committed resolution, the turn's median and worst within their ratchets; at the design
    point, every calendar turn — an ordinary weekday, a Monday, a heavy Monday, three closed days and a quarter-end
    payday, four closed days and an ordinary day — within `[fin.turn]`'s worst, and the median within its median,
    each with 10% headroom under N8.2; a turn that passes without its headroom is a finding. The worst turns carry
    every dated day that can fall on them and a campaign day, and each event on its worst day, one at a time
    (ARCHITECTURE §13.2's composition, `perf/design.toml [fin.calendar]`), against the same worst;
  - **memory** (N8.4): the resident peak at the design point within `[fin.mem]`'s peak, 10% under the owner's
    4.5 GB; bytes a person at the committed resolution within its ratchet;
  - **saves** (N8.4, N8.10): a full save and a restore each within the owner's 5 s (`[fin.save]`); the saves kept,
    with the one being written, within 4 GB;
  - **the run**: the audit reports no finding; every live check passes, or is not yet applicable and listed with the
    run's length (spec Appendix E 39);
  - **placeholders**: every placeholder the stage retires is gone; every one remaining names a later step.
- **The stage's heavy days** *(the gate's own)*: each heavy day the stage's mechanisms add — a month-end billing
  day, a quarter-end, a filing window's busiest day, an election, a busy market day, a resolution's next day — named
  and its time read from the run.
- **The stage's macro reads** *(the gate's own)*: frozen in `data/observer/READS.toml` by the stage's first step, a
  `docs` step, before any other code of the stage; the gate reads them and never writes them. Each is reported
  against real economies with its declared relationship and source (spec Appendix E 25), never tuned (N7).
- **A miss** is a finding, met in N8.7's order: representation and traversal first, then E 41's valves in reverse
  order, each recorded in `perf/design.toml` with its `forced_by`; what remains goes to the owner with its numbers
  (§12). The next stage does not start until the budget in force is met.
- **Done when**: the run (`tools/bench.sh -g`) clean and every criterion holding, or the owner's decision recorded in §12 and the budget
  then in force met; ARCHITECTURE §13 restated with the stage's measured lines; the two independent reviews done;
  the section removed.
- **Not allowed**: tuning; reads chosen after seeing the run; an exit shown by a second run of the world; a gate
  judged off the bench before the owner calls the device run.

## 3. Stage 0 — Foundations

Every step of Stage 0 (S0.01–S0.28) is done. How it is built is recorded in the architecture, and its identifiers
stay in §13 with the clauses they complete.

---

## 4. Stage 1 — The circular flow

### The core: frame and tools (S1.100–S1.133)

The frame every base step is built and judged in. It restates the architecture for the core — its stale sections
retired, the crate map, the day's stage table, the design point, the budgets and the design rules R1–R12 — so that
every base step writes its own section into a skeleton that already stands (design first). It gives the bench its
finished-volume measure (`tools/bench.sh -F`, the `phx-fin` harness, `perf/design.toml`, the counters it reads), sets
the ratchets at the design point (`perf/budget.toml [fin]`), and gives `phx-check` the rules that hold the core's
discipline, each listing today's sites in an exceptions file whose count only falls as the migrations land. None of
these steps changes a mechanism or an outcome of the world.

**Exit**: the architecture describes the core's crates, stages and budgets at the design point with a planned
subsection per core crate; `tools/bench.sh -F all` runs, reports and checks every `[fin.*]` ratchet; the kept kernels
are measured at the design point; `phx-check` refuses maps, whole-table walks, dispatch around the pool, register and
kind reads by name, allocation, bare-slot identities and absent-as-zero on the day's paths, with today's sites
listed; the clause map's L and N rows are machine-checked; the committed resolution's world and its ratchets are
unchanged.

**Placeholders**

| Placeholder | Introduced | Retired by |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `[fin.kept]` ratchets over today's kernels (flows, wheel, posted meeting, hiring's search, calendar, draws) | S1.119 | the base step that replaces each: S1.248 (settlement), S1.225 (the wheel), S1.306 (the retail meeting, K-73), S1.321 (search), S1.178 (day facts), S1.176 (streams) |
| Composite day and turn lines read from declared targets for bases not yet built | S1.116 | each base step's `-F` driver; none remains after S1.360 |
| Exceptions files of PC-92, PC-96–PC-101 listing today's sites | S1.120–S1.130 | retired by S1.492, which empties every exception file; until then each migration step removes its sites, and the listed `core_*.rs` modules are admitted by S1.355 (PC-102), each entry carrying its retiring step |
| `#[saved(skip)]` sites without `rebuild =` in PC-101's exceptions | S1.130 | S1.184 (`UnitIds::plain`), S1.225 (the wheel's scratch), S1.248 (settlement's `Work`), S1.264 (`DatedFamily::alike`), S1.306 (the meeting's scratch), each giving its site a rebuild |
| §7 subsections' "Today" paragraphs describing the code as it stands | S1.100 | each base step's section; S1.360 requires none |

---

### The core: bases (S1.159–S1.360)

#### Memory, execution, foundation, the physical world (S1.159–S1.193)

This group builds the lowest bases of the core, the ones every later base stands on: generation-checked references,
day buffers and the day plan that places them, the save contract's rebuild pass and frame-hash tree, the sum-tree, keyed
indexes kept by events, epoch flags, horizon rings and the interner in `phx-store`; chunk plans, partitioned apply with
its sweep hooks and declared sweeps in `phx-exec`; apportionment, the money viewpoints, identity and unit widths and
the stream families (world, observer, advice) in the foundation; the calendar's day facts, dated policy schedules, the
kind catalogue and its family codes, the units registry and the stage table in `phx-core`; and routes, the day's use of
the network, cells, deposits and weather in `phx-geo`. Each base is designed for its last user in Stages 2–8, measured
alone at the design point by `tools/bench.sh -F <base>`, and followed, where today's code has its own structure, by the
migration that deletes it. The place index (S1.274) is built after the holdings' unit totals (S1.273), where its reads
exist.

**Exit**: every base of S1.159–S1.193 within its `perf/budget.toml [fin.*]` ratchets at the design point; `UnitIds`,
`GoodIds`, the day's hand sequence (`day.rs`), the 46 old sub-steps, the kinds table of
`phx-world/src/consts.rs`, freight's route maps and the weather's own stores deleted; the memory this group states
within ARCHITECTURE §13's lines: line 21 (day buffers) 160.1 MB at the day's maximum (S1.161), line 22 (slack) 57 MB

### S1.163 — The world hash as a tree of frame hashes

**Status**: planned
**Kind**: kernel
**Clauses**: none
**Architecture**: §7.1 (phx-store), "The world hash", written; §11 (Persistence: the world hash) updated.
**Depends on**: S1.162 (the logical hash covers what the save contract calls primary).
**Goal**: the world hash is SipHash-2-4 over each 1 MiB frame of the save's encoded primary columns, combined in a
binary tree whose shape depends only on the number of frames, so frames hash on every worker at once and the hash is the
same however they were hashed.

**Files**:

| path | purpose |
| --- | --- |
| `crates/kernel/phx-store/src/hash.rs` | `FrameHasher`: a hash a frame under `HASH_KEY`; `combine` in a left-balanced tree; `LogicalHasher` kept for tests |
| `crates/kernel/phx-store/src/hash_tests.rs` | unit tests |
| `crates/apps/phx-fin/src/save.rs` | the `-F` driver's hash part (encode and hash the design point's primary state) |
| `perf/budget.toml` | `[fin.save] encode_mb_s_core`, `hash_ms` (added) |
| `docs/ARCHITECTURE.md` | §7.1 "The world hash"; §11 |

**Design**:
- **Frames**: the save's stream of encoded bytes (per-field transforms, bit-packing per 1 024 values, `encode.rs`,
  unchanged) is cut into fixed 1 MiB frames, as the zstd frames already are (`SAVE_FRAME_BYTES`); each frame's
  SipHash-2-4 (128-bit, `HASH_KEY`) is computed by whichever worker compresses it.
- **Tree**: frame hashes are combined pairwise in a left-balanced binary tree over the frame count (a leaf per frame, an
  inner node hashing its two children), so the root depends on the frames' bytes and their order only, never on the
  hashing workers (E7). Only primary columns enter it (a derived index never does, S1.162).
- **Cost**: the sequential `LogicalHasher` over the whole state (`hash.rs`) costs ≈ 2 core-s at the design point
  on one core; the tree spreads it over the save's workers (≈ 0.65 s on three phone cores), inside S1.356's
  `[fin.save] save_ms`.
- **Load**: the loaded frames are hashed the same way and the root held to the manifest's (§11).
- Replaces: the sequential whole-state hash for the world hash; `LogicalHasher` stays for logic-level tests.

**Edge cases**:
- E7: the root is the same for 1–8 hashing workers — `frame_tree_same_for_any_workers`.
- E6: a save's root equals the loaded frames' root — `root_equal_after_load`.
- A frame count that is not a power of two gives a defined, left-balanced tree — `odd_frame_count_tree`.
- E8: a truncated or damaged frame is refused by its decoder before hashing (kept `DecodeError`) —
  `damaged_frame_refused`.

**Extension points**: S1.356 (the world hash as a tree of frame hashes).
**Unit tests**: `frame_tree_same_for_any_workers`, `root_equal_after_load`, `odd_frame_count_tree`,
`damaged_frame_refused`, `hash_covers_primary_only`.
**Live checks**: LC-0-35 (a periodic save's hash held to its manifest) at the gates.
**Budget**:
- Volumes: the save's encoded primary state at the design point (S1.356's `[fin.save] raw_mb`, derived from the
  ledger's saved lines).
- Access: at the declared save moments and at a load, apart from the turn.
- Unit targets: encode ≥ 400 MB/s a core; the frame hash ≥ 1.5 GB/s over three cores.
- `ledger line 23 (save buffers): +0 B (named slot: the frames in flight, S1.356's buffers)`.
- Ratchets: `[fin.save]` `encode_mb_s_core` 400 (added; only rises), `hash_ms` 650 (added).
**Guards**: none new.
**Not allowed**: a hash over a derived index; a sequential hash of the whole state; a tree whose shape depends on the
workers.
**Done when**:
- [ ] `FrameHasher`, the tree and their tests; the fast checks pass.
- [ ] `StoreStats` (S1.117, declared in `phx-store`): none (no store); the hashing counts frames visited into `ExecCounters::visited`, in the
  `phx-exec` traversal that runs them (only `phx-exec` shares a counter across workers).
- [ ] `tools/bench.sh -F save` (encode and hash) at the design point within `[fin.save] encode_mb_s_core`, `hash_ms`.
- [ ] §7.1 "The world hash" and §11 updated; the two reviews done; status `done` and the section removed.

### S1.164 — The sum-tree

**Status**: planned
**Kind**: kernel
**Clauses**: none
**Architecture**: §7.1 (phx-store), "Sum-trees", written.
**Depends on**: S1.160 (the per-worker scratch of a draw's cumulative is a day buffer); S1.162 (trees are derived and
rebuilt at load by the `Rebuild` pass; the round-trip harness).
**Goal**: a pool of Fenwick trees over integer weights in one column, each addressed by (tree, index), with update,
total and prefix-find in O(log n) and removal as weight zero, so no meeting or draw ever rebuilds a table of weights.

**Files**:

| path | purpose |
| --- | --- |
| `crates/kernel/phx-store/src/sumtree.rs` | `SumTrees`: headers, weights, `update`, `total`, `find`, `push`, capacity classes |
| `crates/kernel/phx-store/src/sumtree_tests.rs` | unit tests against a plain prefix-sum over hand-built weights |
| `crates/apps/phx-fin/src/stalls.rs` | the `-F` driver (the stalls of `[store] stalls` in trees per (good, zone)) |
| `perf/budget.toml` | `[fin.stalls] update_ns` kept; `[fin.sumtree]` (added) |
| `docs/ARCHITECTURE.md` | §7.1 "Sum-trees" |

**Design**:
- Layout: a `Column<u64>` of weights holding every tree's Fenwick array; a `Column<TreeHeader>` (offset u32, len u32,
  capacity class u8, the tree's total cached as u64; 16 B). A tree's capacity is a class of 4 · 2ᵏ entries; a tree that
  fills moves to the next class (copy O(n), amortised O(1) a push); freed extents return to a free list per class.
- `update(tree, i, Δ: i64)`: the Fenwick walk `i += i & -i`, checked `u64` arithmetic; a total past `u64::MAX` is
  `capacity_exceeded!` (E8). `set(tree, i, w)` = update by the difference. `total(tree)` one read.
- `find(tree, x: u64) -> i`: binary lifting from the highest power of two ≤ len, O(log n): the least i whose prefix sum
  exceeds x. With `x` drawn uniform below `total` from the caller's stream, `find` is a draw proportional to weight.
- Removal is `set(i, 0)`: the index keeps its place (positions are stable, so a member's stored position stays valid);
  a tree whose zero entries pass half its length is re-packed at its owner's next apply point, the owner rewriting its
  members' positions (S1.165's weighted mode).
- Total 0 is an answer, not an error: `find` on an empty or all-zero tree returns `Missing` and the caller records the
  failed meeting (MKT.10).
- Weights are integers the owner declares (a stall's weight is its price term quantised by the market's declared scale,
  S1.301): sums are exact and order-free, so any worker count gives the same draws.
- Concurrency: a tree is written by one worker at a time (its market key's job); a meeting reads its own updates only.
- Save/load: `#[saved(skip, rebuild = …)]`: trees are rebuilt from their owners' rows at load in slot order (S1.162).
- Replaces: the posted meeting's per-round `remake` of alias tables (`phx-market/src/meet.rs`) — adopted by S1.301 and
  S1.306.

**Edge cases**:
- E2: an all-zero tree draws nothing — `find_on_zero_total_is_missing`.
- E8: a total past `u64::MAX` stops — `total_overflow_stops`.
- E7: `find` depends on weights and `x` only — `find_is_exact_inverse_of_prefix`.
- E6: a tree rebuilt from its owner's rows equals the saved world's sums — `rebuild_equals_incremental` (through
  `roundtrip`).
- E1: a day's sold-out removals are `set(i, 0)` at O(log n) each, positions kept — `removal_keeps_positions`.

**Extension points**: S1.165 (weighted instances keep their members' weights in a sum-tree); S1.188 (the lot's draws
over crossing pairs); S1.301 (the sum-tree kernel); S1.306 (the sum-tree); S1.307 (count sum-trees); S2.211 (K-05: the
draw, built for the event and released at the close); S6.122 (sum-trees: a uniform member drawn by `find`).
**Unit tests**: `prefix_sums_match_plain`, `find_is_exact_inverse_of_prefix`, `find_on_zero_total_is_missing`,
`total_overflow_stops`, `class_growth_keeps_sums`, `removal_keeps_positions`, `rebuild_equals_incremental`.
**Live checks**: none.
**Budget**:
- Volumes: the stalls of `perf/design.toml [store] stalls` in trees per (good, zone): ≈ 250 k keys at `[resolution]
  zones` 1 000 (500 k at 2 000); reprices and sold-out removals `[day.*] reprices`, `removals`; finds
  inside the retail match (`[day.*] retail`).
- Access: event-driven (a reprice, a sale that sells out, a draw).
- Unit targets: update ≤ 46 VM ns (k 1.3, miss budget ≤ 0.3); find inside `fin.retail.match_ns`.
- Bytes: 8 B a weight at ≤ 1.4 class slack, 16 B a tree header (`[fin.sumtree] bytes_per_weight`), so ≈ 4 MB of headers
  at 1 000 zones (8 at 2 000); the stalls' MB is S1.301's line-17 figure, not stated here.
- Ratchets: `[fin.stalls] update_ns` 46; `[fin.sumtree]` (added) `find_ns` 15, `bytes_per_weight` 12.
**Guards**: none new (PC-92 covers `phx-store`).
**Not allowed**: a table of weights rebuilt per round or per call; floating weights; a removal that shifts positions.
**Done when**:
- [ ] `SumTrees` and its tests; the fast checks pass.
- [ ] `StoreStats` (S1.117, declared in `phx-store`) implemented for the trees; finds and updates count rows visited into `ExecCounters::visited`, in the
  `phx-exec` traversal that runs them (only `phx-exec` shares a counter across workers).
- [ ] `tools/bench.sh -F stalls` (the sum-tree part) at the design point within `[fin.stalls] update_ns` and
      `[fin.sumtree]`.
- [ ] §7.1 "Sum-trees" written; the two reviews done; status `done` and the section removed.
